description: A pinch at the front of the hip when you squat deep or lift your knee is your hip asking for room. Today you measure your rotation with a simple knee-to-floor test, learn what the pinch actually means, and start giving the socket its space back.

scenes.narration: Lie on your back with both knees bent and feet flat. Take one foot and rest it across the opposite knee, like the start of a figure four. Now let the raised knee fall outward, away from you, as far as it travels on its own. No pushing it down, no forcing. Measure the gap between that knee and the floor by stacking your fists in the space. How many fists fit? That is your number for this side. Then switch. Two numbers, and if you live with a pinching hip, one side will measure very differently from the other. Write them down. At the end of this video I will tell you what the gap is really reporting about the deepest joint in your body.

scenes.label: THE LINE FOR HIP ROTATION
scenes.narration: Here is the line. Two fists of gap is where a guarded hip becomes an open one. Four fists or more means the rotation system has been quietly shutting down, usually for years, and the pinch you feel in deep positions is its way of asking for room. One fist means the knee nearly rests on the floor, the range athletes and dancers take for granted. But as with every two-sided test on this channel, the gap between your sides matters as much as the gap to the floor. Hips are supposed to be a matched pair. When one rotates freely and the other stops halfway, every squat, lunge and flight of stairs is negotiated asymmetrically, and the pinch is the sound of the negotiation failing.
scenes.sub: 4+ fists: rotation shutting down - 1 fist: wide open

beats.text: THE DEEPEST BALL AND SOCKET YOU OWN
THE PINCH IS A SPACE PROBLEM
RANGE IS ROOM, AND ROOM RETURNS

scenes.narration: Understand the joint you are measuring. The hip is a deep ball and socket, built to rotate before it does anything else. A baby explores rotation before walking. A martial artist's kick, a dancer's turnout and your own ability to sit cross-legged all run on the same rotary range you just measured. The pinch at the front of the hip, the sharp little nip when you squat deep, pull your knee to your chest or sit in a low car, usually means the ball is running out of room in the socket as it moves, and the soft tissues at the front are getting compressed in the closing gap. It feels alarming, but in most cases it is a space and control problem, not a damage report. The tissues around the hip, capsule, ligaments and the deep rotator muscles with their tendons, adapt to the ranges they are used in. A hip that has not rotated fully in years literally organizes itself around the smaller range. The good news hidden in that sentence is the whole episode: tissue that organized itself small can organize itself open again, given patient, repeated invitations to the full range.

beats.text: THE DEEP ROTATORS ARE THE CREW

lines: Six small muscles steer the ball
and keep it centered as it turns.
beats.title: THE STEERING CREW

scenes.narration: Room alone is not the goal, and this is where most hip advice goes wrong. Wrapped around the back of the socket sit six small muscles, the deep rotators, whose tendons steer the ball and keep it centered while the hip turns. If those are asleep, extra range is just extra wobble, and the joint will guard it away again within weeks. This is why stretching alone so often disappoints: it borrows room without hiring the crew to manage it. The approach in this video pairs the two. Gentle, repeated rotation visits the full range, telling the tissues the room is wanted. Slow, controlled work in that range, like the horse stance and deep squat positions from earlier in this series, wakes the steering crew up inside it. Room plus steering equals range you actually own. Your fist measurement tracks the room. Your control in deep positions tracks the crew. A healed hip needs both numbers moving.

The usual suspect is behind this one as well. Sitting holds the hip at ninety degrees, in neutral rotation, for most of the modern day. The capsule and deep tissues adapt to exactly that: a joint that is excellent at being a chair joint and increasingly foreign to every other position. Then life asks for rotation without warning: getting out of a low car, a deep squat to lift a box, a twist on a football field, and the unprepared joint pinches or guards. The antidote is not a heroic weekly stretch. It is daily, brief, complete range: a few minutes where the hip visits its corners the way a tongue visits a sore tooth, gently and often. Floors help. Sitting on the floor in varied positions while you watch or read is passive range work that cultures without chairs get for free. Your hip does not need a program with a name. It needs its full map back, visited daily, until the map feels like home again.

beats.text: LESS MASS IN THE SOCKET'S WAY

scenes.narration: Here is the skinny advantage in the socket. Deep hip positions, the squats and floor sits that restore this joint, are loaded by your bodyweight, and a lighter frame makes every one of them cheaper and safer to practice daily. Heavy men often have to ration deep position work because each visit costs their joints more. You can live in these positions, a few minutes at a time, spread across every day, which is precisely the dosage this tissue responds to. The floor is your clinic and it charges you less than it charges almost anyone else. All it asks is that you actually get down there.

Now we visit the full map together. On your back, figure four, let the knee fall and breathe into the end of the range for a few slow breaths, then lift it back with control. Thirty seconds per side, four rounds. No forcing, ever. The knee travels where it wants to today. Rotate. Go.

Here is your week. Rotation visits daily, in the rounds you just did, plus floor sitting in varied positions whenever life allows, and horse stance or deep squat holds twice a week for the steering crew. Now the mistakes. Mistake one: pushing the knee down with your hand to win range. That is how a space problem becomes an irritation problem. The knee falls where it falls, and gravity is the only coach allowed. Mistake two: training through a true pinch, the sharp nip at the front during the movement itself. A stretch feeling in the buttock is the work. A pinch at the front is a stop sign for that angle today. Mistake three: expecting symmetry in a week. Hips remodel on a schedule of months, and if hip pain persists, limits your walking, or ever comes with clicking that locks, see a professional and have the joint examined properly. Half a fist a month is real progress here. Sockets open slowly, and then they stay open.

scenes.label: RETEST - SAME FLOOR, NO FORCING
scenes.narration: So, your numbers, and this time we grade the bigger gap, because that is the side that needs the work. Four fists or more: rotation has been shutting down for a long time, and now it has a daily invitation to reopen. Two to four: the socket is organizing itself open, keep visiting. Two fists: the line, an open hip by any honest standard. One fist: wide open, the range of a man who lives on the floor and moves like it. Put the bigger gap in the comments, and tell us which side it was. In thirty days we measure the fists again.
scenes.sub: comment your bigger gap - and the side

scenes.narration: Thirty days from now the same knee will fall a little further toward the same floor, quietly, the way all real healing happens. Subscribe so the retest finds you, and leave the bigger gap in the comments where you cannot hide from it. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: Your Hip Rotation Test Reveals the Truth About Your hip tissue healing
